papers.title: Mechanistic classification of the AAA superfamily with protein language models
papers.abstract: The ATPases Associated with various cellular Activities (AAA) superfamily utilizes a conserved three-dimensional structure to drive diverse mechanical workflows. While cryo-electron microscopy has revealed extensive structural data, predicting how specific sequence variations dictate unique biochemical mechanisms remains a challenge. Here, we present a machine learning framework to resolve these sequence-function relationships by mapping the functional landscape of AAA proteins. We established a hierarchical classification scheme based on five distinct modes of coupling ATP hydrolysis to mechanical work. Using CatFunc, a lightweight protein language model (PLM) pipeline, we leveraged evolutionary context from proteomic sequences for supervised classification of these mechanisms. Validation studies demonstrated excellent recall of our mechanistic annotations across the AAA hierarchy. Notably, systematic misclassifications revealed a shared evolutionary and mechanistic ancestry within the rotary motor class. Applying the model to out-of-distribution proteomic datasets, we established biophysical metrics to detect unrepresented functions, demonstrating that restricting inference to isolated AAA domains significantly improves classification accuracy for novel sequences. Our framework provides a scalable strategy for decoding functional phenotypes from sequence data, offering a transferable approach for other biomedically vital families like G protein-coupled receptors and kinases.

papers.title: The bacterial iron sensor IdeR distinguishes DNA sequences by applying stress to non-cognate DNA
papers.abstract: The transcription factor IdeR regulates iron homeostasis in many gram-positive bacteria. It primarily functions as a repressor of iron uptake genes by binding to their promoters and blocking RNA polymerase access. IdeR recognizes a highly conserved DNA sequence consisting of four palindromic 5'-C1C2T3A4A5 repeats. For target site recognition, IdeR requires a thymine in position 3 of the repeat and at least one cytosine in the first two positions, while the identity of the bases in positions 4 and 5 is less important. We have previously shown that IdeR recognizes its target sequences through indirect or shape readout, rather than direct interactions with the bases. However, the mechanism of indirect recognition is unknown. Here we employed molecular dynamics simulations, X-ray crystallography, and DNA-binding assays to investigate the thermodynamic principles underlying accurate pyrimidine recognition by IdeR. We found that the recognition helix of IdeR forms a differential dielectric cleft that accommodates the C-H edge of the 5'-C1C2T3 sequence, with a polar pocket for the first two bases and a non-polar pocket for the third. The local dielectric environment of IdeR applies strain to non-cognate DNA, leading to non-productive binding and thereby ensuring the fidelity of target DNA reading.

papers.title: A circRNA-derived IRES-like element enables programmable translational activation of the endogenous chaperone HSP90
papers.abstract: Circular RNAs (circRNAs) are covalently closed transcripts that lack a 5' cap, consequently their translation depends on cap-independent initiation, in most cases through Internal Ribosome Entry Sites (IRESs). Whereas IRES-mediated translation has been studied almost exclusively in cis, the use of IRES-containing circRNAs to activate translation of an independent mRNA in trans has only recently begun to be explored. Here, we characterize SynFarsa, a synthetic circRNA-derived IRES-like element that promotes cap-lindependent translation in mouse and human cells. We engineered SynFarsa into a trans-acting regulator by fusing it to a short antisense sequence complementary to a selected region of a target mRNA. This reproduces the architecture of a circular SINEUP, in which IRES activity promotes translation in trans of a transcript recognized through antisense complementarity. Directing this construct to the hsp90 3'UTR increased HSP90 protein levels approximately 1.6-lfold without altering hsp90 mRNA abundance, whereas the hsp70 3'UTR and the 5'UTRs of both transcripts were not permissive, indicating that activity depends strongly on target site selection. In a FUSP525L neuroblastoma model of Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis, this increase in HSP90 was accompanied by a reduction in the number and size of cytoplasmic FUS aggregates. SynFarsa thus provides a circRNA-derived effector domain for targeted translational upregulation of an endogenous protein.

papers.title: Tropomodulin and Leiomodin Differentially Nucleate Tropomyosin Assembly on Actin Filaments
papers.abstract: Tropomyosins play a central role in the regulation of the actin cytoskeleton by assembling along filaments into rope-like, head-to-tail polymers ("clusters") along filaments that regulate the binding and activity of numerous actin-binding proteins. Importantly, in cells, tropomyosins do not decorate actin filaments uniformly; some filaments are devoid of tropomyosins, whereas others recruit specific isoforms. To explore the diversity of tropomyosin-isoform binding kinetics and identify factors that control their assembly, we designed tropomyosin constructs, bearing a natural N-terminal acetylation and targeted cysteine mutations for fluorescence labelling. We analysed the binding of different tropomyosin isoforms to individual actin filaments reconstituted inside a microfluidic chamber. We show that, despite significant differences in spontaneous nucleation and elongation rates, all tested tropomyosin isoforms can coassemble within the same clusters. In addition, we identified tropomodulin and leiomodin, two pointed-end-binding proteins, to efficiently nucleate the formation of tropomyosin clusters on actin filaments, for all tested tropomyosin isoforms. Notably, while tropomodulin nucleates tropomyosin clusters from the pointed end, leiomodin does so along the entire filament.

papers.title: Evolution and remodeling of acceptor specificity in the NodZ α-1,6-fucosyltransferase
papers.abstract: Glycosyltransferases have broad diversity in their acceptor substrates, yet the molecular and evolutionary basis of this diversity remains poorly understood. NodZ is an -1,6-fucosyltransferase that fucosylates Nod factors, lipochitooligosaccharide molecules involved in the establishment of rhizobium-legume symbioses. While NodZ is the only known bacterial member of the GT23 family of -1,6-fucosyltransferases, the determinants of its acceptor selectivity and the evolutionary origins thereof are unclear. Here, a phylogenetic analysis of 332 NodZ-like proteins revealed a distinct rhizobial clade and significantly greater structural diversity in the N-terminus than in the C-terminus. Kinetic analysis of a Mesorhizobium japonicum NodZ demonstrated selectivity for longer chitooligosaccharide acceptors (comprised of four to five GlcNAc units), while alanine scanning revealed W139 as a primary determinant of this chain length preference. We propose that W139 forms an aromatic platform that engages distal GlcNAc units present only in longer acceptors, coupling productive binding to acceptor chain length. We then used the NodZ phylogeny to reconstruct ancestral NodZ homolog sequences, which indicated that W139 emerged at the base of the rhizobial clade, and thus may represent a key evolutionary step towards canonical NodZ function. Additionally, the most recent resurrected ancestor was capable of fucosylating chitooligosaccharides with lower efficiency than the extant NodZ, suggesting that efficiency towards chitooligosaccharides was improved during the evolution of this family. Results described here demonstrate that evolutionary diversification of the N-terminal region can remodel acceptor specificity while preserving the conserved catalytic architecture of GT23 fucosyltransferases, providing a framework for understanding and engineering fucosyltransferase specificity.

papers.title: Structural basis of eIF4E recognition of synthetic mRNA 5' cap analogues links cap architecture to affinity and biological activity
papers.abstract: Eukaryotic mRNAs carry a 5'-terminal 7-methylguanosine (m7G) cap that is recognized by multiple cellular proteins and is essential for mRNA self-discrimination, stability, and translation. The eukaryotic translation initiation factor 4E (eIF4E) binds the 5' cap and promotes recruitment of mRNAs to the ribosomal translation initiation complex, a critical step in cap-dependent translation. Beyond naturally occurring cap modifications that modulate mRNA interactions and fate, non-natural 5' cap modifications can be used to finely tune diverse aspects of mRNA biology. This has gained particular relevance with the emergence of in vitro transcribed mRNAs as a powerful therapeutic modality for protein replacement therapies and vaccines. Here, we report binding data for a series of synthetic 5' cap analogues interacting with eIF4E, together with X-ray crystal structures of eIF4E-cap complexes, providing detailed insights into the structural determinants of cap recognition by eIF4E. Furthermore, analysis of gene expression from mRNAs carrying different synthetic cap analogues in human cell lines and mice revealed a relationship between cap architecture and protein expression. Taken together, our structural, biochemical, and functional data establish structure-activity relationships for synthetic cap analogues and identify structural features associated with enhanced translational performance.

papers.title: β-Hairpin Fold Peptide Brush Polymers
papers.abstract: Peptide-brush polymers prepared via graft-through polymerization of peptide-based olefinic monomers form Protein-Like Polymers (PLPs) with demonstrated utility as chemical biology tools for modulating intracellular protein--protein interactions and are in development as a emerging class of therapeutic. This favorable bioactivity has been achieved in part by mimicking some of the structural and functional features of proteins, such as their dynamic, globular solution-phase structures, ability to insert into lipid membranes and enter cells, and tendency to enforce -helicity in peptide side chains. However, because structure leads to function, insight into the structure of these proteomimetic polymers, particularly their overall tertiary structure and the extent to which this influences the brush peptide structure, is incomplete. To further this understanding, we prepared a set of brush polymers incorporating the trpzip2 peptide sequence, commonly used as a model system for protein folding. We examine these polymers via circular dichroism spectroscopy, infrared spectroscopy, and small-angle X-ray scattering, coupled with insights from molecular dynamics simulations. Here, a loss of the {beta}-hairpin structure of the monomer is observed regardless of polymer composition, and simulations corroborate that the polymer backbone destabilizes local secondary structure, restricting peptide motion and altering the accessible free-energy landscape. This study provides insight into design rules governing these synthetic polymer-based proteomimetics.

papers.title: Tertiary structure of a Nif11-like leader peptide mediates protein-protein interactions with a RiPP biosynthetic enzyme
papers.abstract: Ribosomally synthesized and post-translationally modified peptides (RiPPs) are produced from precursor peptides that typically contain a short, unstructured N-terminal leader region that engages RiPP biosynthetic enzymes through peptide-protein contacts. A distinct subclass of leader peptides, the nitrogen-fixing protein 11-like leader peptides (Nif11-LPs), are unusually long and conspicuously enriched in cyanobacteria. No atomic structures of Nif11-LPs have been reported. Here, we report the solution structure of MppEleader, a Nif11-LP from the marine cyanobacterium Moorena producens PAL. MppEleader adopts a bipartite architecture with a rigid N-terminal tetrahelical bundle stabilized around a hydrophobic nucleus, followed by a dynamic, largely disordered C-terminal region containing a conserved L(X)L motif. We show that the -ketoglutarate/non-heme iron enzyme MppG dihydroxylates the macrocyclized MppEcore peptide in a strictly leader-dependent manner. NMR titrations and structure-guided mutagenesis demonstrate that both the tetrahelical hydrophobic nucleus and the L(X)L motif of MppE make direct, functionally required contacts with MppG, including its RiPP recognition element (RRE) domain. An AlphaFold3-guided structural model rationalizes these contacts. Together, these findings establish a tertiary structure-dependent protein-protein interaction paradigm for RiPP core peptide modification, distinguishing Nif11-LP recognition from canonical short-leader mechanisms and expanding the understanding of substrate recognition in RiPP biosynthesis.

papers.title: Ambient-Condition Visualization of Metalloenzyme Reactive Intermediates Enabled by the SHINERS Paradigm
papers.abstract: Reactive metal-oxygen intermediates are central to metalloenzyme catalysis, yet their low populations and short lifetimes make vibrational characterization under aqueous reaction conditions challenging. Here, we establish shell-isolated nanoparticle-enhanced Raman spectroscopy (SHINERS) as a powerful vibrational approach for visualizing reaction-associated metal-ligand signatures of reactive metalloenzyme states. Across the heme and non-heme iron enzymes TauD, VioC, CYP119, and TqaLNc, isotope-sensitive features provide vibrational information on reactive coordination states. In TauD and VioC, isotope-sensitive features provide vibrational characterization of Fe(IV)=O intermediates. In CYP119, an isotope-sensitive Fe(IV)=O vibration is assigned to P450 Compound I generated by m-CPBA, including under lauric-acid turnover conditions. Most notably, in TqaLNc, combined 18O- and 15N-sensitive vibrational responses support formation of the proposed (R)HN-Fe(IV)=O coordination state and the dynamic-coordination mechanism underlying selective C-N bond formation. These results demonstrate that SHINERS can serve as a powerful technique for the in situ vibrational visualization of reactive intermediates and their coordination states in metalloenzyme catalysis.

papers.title: HNRNPM promotes protein synthesis via an interaction with stem-loop 5 in the SARS-CoV-2 5'-UTR
papers.abstract: The 5'-untranslated region (5'-UTR) of severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2) is highly structured and comprises five conserved stem-loops that serve as cis-acting regulatory elements. During infection, host proteins are recruited to these elements and regulate multiple steps during the viral life cycle. Stem-loop 5 (SL5) is highly conserved among different alpha- and betacoronaviruses and includes the start codon of non-structural protein 1 (nsp1). However, the function of SL5 in viral replication and its interacting proteins remain to be determined. Here, we identified heterogeneous nuclear ribonucleoprotein M (HNRNPM) as a host protein functionally interacting with SL5. HNRNPM translocates into the cytoplasm during SARS-CoV-2 infection and promotes protein synthesis from the viral 5'-UTR. Mutations in the lower stem of SL5 impair HNRNPM binding and reduce protein synthesis. Notably, the interaction between HNRNPM and SL5 is conserved among different alpha- and betacoronaviruses. Our findings indicate that HNRNPM is an important host factor that regulates viral translation to promote SARS-CoV-2 replication.

papers.title: Long-form hibernation-promoting factor coordinates 100S assembly and translational repression
papers.abstract: Ribosome hibernation mediated by long-form hibernation-promoting factor (HPF) requires coordination of ribosome dimerization and translational repression, but how these functions are integrated remains unclear. Here, we present cryo-EM structures of native 100S from a deep-sea Bacillus isolate, revealing a conformationally heterogeneous 100S population. Beyond the established roles of the HPF N-terminal domain (NTD) in decoding-center occlusion and the C-terminal domain (CTD) in dimerization, our analyses reveal additional contributions from the Linker and a charged CTD surface near the 16S rRNA 3' terminus containing the anti-Shine-Dalgarno (aSD) sequence. Linker substitutions differentially affect translational repression while retaining 100S formation, with distinct effects of the two Linker segments. Mutation of the charged CTD surface enhances translational repression while retaining robust 100S formation, suggesting an additional role beyond CTD-mediated ribosome dimerization. Functional analyses in an E. coli cell-free translation system further show that the inhibitory activity of individual HPF regions varies with translational context. Together, these findings support a modular model in which the NTD, Linker, and CTD make distinct but interconnected contributions to 100S assembly and translational repression.

papers.title: C-terminal domain of SARS CoV 2 nucleocapsid protein binds transcriptional regulatory sequence RNA with high affinity and forms higher-order assemblies
papers.abstract: The SARS-CoV-2 nucleocapsid (N) protein is a 419-amino-acid modular protein essential for viral RNA replication, genome packaging, and host-cell modulation. It contains two structured domains, the N-terminal RNA-binding domain (NTD) and C-terminal dimerization domain (CTD), separated and flanked by three intrinsically disordered regions. Although the CTD mediates N-protein dimerization and contributes to RNA binding, the molecular basis of its interaction with RNA remains poorly understood. Here, we characterized CTD binding to transcriptional regulatory sequence (TRS) RNAs from the SARS-CoV-2 genome using NMR spectroscopy, isothermal titration calorimetry, size-exclusion chromatography, and in vitro phase-separation assays. The CTD bound structured stem-loop TRS RNA with higher affinity than the canonical RNA-binding NTD. NMR chemical-shift perturbation experiments indicated formation of higher-order molecular assemblies upon titration of the CTD with longer, structured stem-loop TRS RNA, consistent with size-exclusion chromatography results. The CTD also underwent RNA-induced phase separation in vitro, with stem-loop TRS RNA promoting markedly more robust condensation than single-stranded RNA sequences. Together, these findings establish the CTD as a high-affinity, structure-selective RNA-binding domain with a preference for stem-loop TRS RNA. The results further show that CTD-TRS interactions promote higher-order assembly and phase separation, providing mechanistic insight into N-protein-mediated viral genome packaging and nucleocapsid assembly.

papers.title: Mycothiazole enables structural characterization of entire ubiquinone-accessing tunnel in mitochondrial respiratory complex I
papers.abstract: Mitochondrial NADH-ubiquinone (UQ) oxidoreductase (respiratory complex I) reduces UQ within its long tunnel-like cavity, which is coupled to triggering proton translocation at the membrane domain. Although mammalian complex I adopts distinct "open" and "closed" conformations, the architecture of the UQ-accessing tunnel in the open conformation remains poorly defined owing to partial disorder of the UQ catalytic region near Fe-S cluster N2 in the tunnel. Here, we applied cryo-electron microscopy (EM) single particle analysis to determine the structures of complex I in bovine heart submitochondrial particles in the presence or absence of a mycothiazole-type inhibitor. Preceding photoaffinity labeling experiments using a synthetic photoreactive derivative ([125I]pMT) revealed that mycothiazole specifically labels the 49-kDa and ND1 subunits, both of which form a part of the UQ-accessing tunnel. Cryo-EM analysis demonstrated that bound mycothiazole reorganizes and stabilizes the UQ catalytic region in both open and closed conformations, enabling the first complete structural modeling of the entire UQ-accessing tunnel in the open conformation. Unexpectedly, in the presence of bound mycothiazole, loops of the PSST subunit forming the catalytic region in the tunnel adopted closed conformation-like features, whereas open conformation-like features were determined for the transmembrane helices of ND1 and ND6 subunits. The present study revealed that bound mycothiazole can reorganize the UQ catalytic region in the UQ-accessing tunnel and lead to a hybrid conformational state beyond the canonical open-versus-closed conformational model.

papers.title: Coumarin-based blue excitable probe for functional screening of dehalogenase activity
papers.abstract: In the enzymatic toolbox of depollution, hydrolytic dehalogenases are of particular interest for the bioremediation of organohalogenated compounds. To better identify and characterize these enzymes, it is important to develop appropriate sensing methods. Fluorescent probes for dehalogenase detection have been developed in the past years, however, to this date none were available for application using the common FITC parameters (i.e. excitation laser at 488 nm). To address this limitation, we herein report a new fluorescent probe, COU4-Cl, excitable in the violet (405 nm) and blue (488 nm) wavelengths adapted for the detection and characterization of haloalkane dehalogenases. Its applicability is discussed and evaluated in comparison to the previously described COU2-Cl probe only excitable in the violet (405 nm). This study shows the advantages and complementarity of the two probes, and further demonstrate their application for the discrimination of dehalogenase activity in whole cell assays.

papers.title: Covalent Solvatochromic Membrane Probe for Sensing Lipid Surrounding of Proteins
papers.abstract: Plasma membranes (PM) have been traditionally studied by fluorescent probes by either labelling lipid or protein parts. Based on our MemGraft concept, we report a fluorescent probe based on solvatochromic dye Nile Red (MemGraft-NR) for sensing lipid organization in the immediate surrounding of proteins, i.e. at the protein-lipid interface. Two sequentially attached MemGraft scaffolds are required to ensure robust grafting of Nile Red to PM. In contrast to classical lipid-bound membrane probes, MemGraft-NR exhibits high resistance to the presence of serum and fixation with permeabilization. Two-color confocal imaging of MemGraft-NR in live cells reveals higher polarity at the protein-lipid interface compared to lipid-bound probe NR12A. Surprisingly, MemGraft-NR displays higher sensitivity to variation of cholesterol content in PM compared to NR12A, suggesting that protein-lipid interface is particularly impacted by changes in the lipid composition. MemGraft-NR also enabled in situ monitoring of lipid exchange and permeabilization of PM, something impossible for classical solvatochromic PM probes. Unexpectedly, MemGraft-NR reveals a dramatic decrease in the local polarity in early endosomes, suggesting that endosomal negative curvature provides strong impact on organization of the protein-lipid interface. The developed probe opens a new way to study biological membranes by sensing lipid surrounding of membrane proteins.

papers.title: Heterotypic Condensate Formation by Prion Proteins and Pro-Inflammatory S100A9
papers.abstract: Liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS) of biomacromolecules has been shown to influence a large variety of biological processes via the formation of membraneless organelles. Aberrant LLPS, however, has been implicated in a number of oncological and neurodegenerative disorders. Proteins related to Alzheimer's, Parkinson's diseases and other major amyloidoses have all been shown to form these condensates. Interestingly, some amyloidogenic proteins were demonstrated to form heterotypic droplets, where both molecules coexisted within the same condensate and affected each other's aggregation. While such cross-interactions have been reported numerous times under non-LLPS conditions, the heterotypic droplet assemblies were only shown for a very limited number of amyloidogenic proteins. In this work, we examine heterotypic LLPS of prion proteins and the pro-inflammatory S100A9, whose cross-interaction under non-LLPS conditions we confirmed in a previous work. The results show that this interaction under condensation-promoting conditions enhances their aggregation, leading to the formation of a higher concentration of amyloid structures. These findings suggest that the pro-inflammatory S100A9 may have a critical role in promoting prion protein aggregation via the assembly of heterotypic condensates under high molecular crowding conditions.

papers.title: High-yield expression and purification of the non-phosphorylated form of Human CaMKIIα Kinase
papers.abstract: Human Ca2+/calmodulin (CaM)-dependent protein kinase II alpha (CaMKII) is a highly abundant and conserved protein in the brain. It is a multifunctional serine/threonine kinase that phosphorylates cellular substrates across subcellular compartments, activating signaling pathways essential for long-term memory storage. However, a detailed understanding of protein structure and enzyme-substrate interaction mechanisms require a method to produce active, stable, and pure proteins at scale. Since phosphorylation can alter catalytic activity and substrate affinity, examining the non-phosphorylated state enables an unbiased characterization of basal enzymatic function. Therefore, producing the non-phosphorylated form of the kinase is important for biochemical and structural studies aimed at understanding kinase activation mechanisms. We describe a detailed protocol for the expression and high-yield purification of full-length, non-phosphorylated human CaMKII in bacterial cells. CaMKII was co-expressed with {lambda}-phosphatase to maintain it in a non-phosphorylated state. Protein expression was induced by autoinduction at low temperature to enhance the stability and solubility of CaMKII. Recombinant CaMKII was purified by Ni-NTA affinity chromatography, followed by gel filtration chromatography. Although CaMKII has been considered difficult to purify in its non-phosphorylated form, we obtained it in high yield, and the protein was predominantly non-phosphorylated. Our results show that combining co-expression with autoinduction improves both the solubility and yield of the homogeneous non-phosphorylated form of CaMKII, which could be suitable for subsequent biochemical and structural studies.

papers.title: Glycation proteomics identifies creatine kinase as a mediator of the effects of methylglyoxal on mitochondrial permeability transition
papers.abstract: Opening of the mitochondrial permeability transition (PT) pore is an important step in necrotic cell death in various pathologic conditions such as ischemia-reperfusion injury. Methylglyoxal (MGO) is a byproduct of glycolysis that covalently modifies proteins (i.e., glycation) and is widely regarded as toxic (glycative stress), contributing to the pathology of diabetes. Paradoxically, MGO has been shown to inhibit PT pore opening, but the mechanism of this effect is poorly understood. Herein we show that glycation is elevated in various cardioprotective scenarios. Furthermore, building on a serendipitous finding of the ability of phosphate to block MGO's effect on the PT pore, we used proteomics to map potential sites mediating this effect. From this analysis, mitochondrial creatine kinase (CK) emerged as a phosphate-sensitive MGO target with links to the PT pore. Although MGO inhibited CK activity, this did not appear to be important for its effect on the PT pore. Rather, MGO modified sites on CK that are important for its membrane binding, which likely mediates the combined effects of MGO and phosphate on the PT pore. Furthermore, a consensus sequence for MGO modifications in mitochondria is reported.

papers.title: KPB82 potently and selectively inhibits ACER2 and protects tumor and primary cells from doxorubicin-induced cytotoxicity
papers.abstract: Alkaline ceramidase 2 (ACER2) catalyzes the hydrolysis of ceramides into sphingosine and free fatty acids, playing crucial roles in regulating various biological processes, including but not limited to cell proliferation, survival, and the DNA damage response. However, a pharmacological tool that regulates its catalytic and signaling functions remains to be developed. In this study, N-[(1S,2R)-1-hydroxy-1-phenylpropan-2-yl]dodecane-1-sulfonamide (KPB82) was identified as a potent and selective ACER2 inhibitor. In vitro enzymatic assays showed that KPB82 inhibited ACER2 with an IC50 of 190 nM, while displaying minimal activity against acid and neutral ceramidases (IC50> 100 {micro}M) and no significant inhibition of alkaline ceramidase 1 or alkaline ceramidase 3. Enzymatic kinetic studies revealed that KPB82 is a competitive inhibitor of ACER2. The three-dimensional structure of ACER2 was modeled in the AlphaFold3 server, revealing key Zn2+-coordinating histidine residues and a substrate-binding pocket. Molecular docking studies demonstrated that KPB82 binds ACER2 within this pocket, forming hydrogen bonds with the catalytically important amino residues, Asp93 and His215, and interacting with several hydrophobic residues. Lactate dehydrogenase release assays revealed that KPB82 significantly reduced cytotoxicity in HeLa cells overexpressing ACER2, as well as in HCT116 cells, RT4 cells, and human umbilical vein endothelial cells treated with the DNA-damaging agent doxorubicin. Lipidomic analysis showed that KPB82 inhibited sphingosine production in response to ACER2 overexpression or doxorubicin treatment. Collectively, these findings demonstrate that KPB82 is a potent and selective ACER2 inhibitor capable of suppressing ACER2-dependent biological processes and highlight its potential as a tool for studying ceramide metabolism and ACER2-mediated signaling pathways.

papers.title: Molecular Determinants of G Protein Subtype-Specific Coupling to the Angiotensin II Type 1 Receptor
papers.abstract: Many G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs) are capable of activating multiple heterotrimeric G protein subtypes. The angiotensin II type 1 receptor (AT1R) couples to both Gq and Gi family members, and the two families mediate distinct aspects of the effects of angiotensin II (AngII) on blood pressure and fluid balance. Previous work has pointed to fundamental differences in the strength and ligand-dependence of Gq versus Gi activation by AT1R. Here we resolve key aspects of the mechanisms underlying these subtype-specific patterns of G protein coupling to AT1R. Using cellular biosensors, we show that AT1R activates Gq more efficaciously than Gi. Leveraging mini-G proteins, engineered versions of G subunits that diverge only in the C-terminal 5 helix, we identify four residues dispersed throughout the 5 helix that are sufficient to account for these differences. We employ radioligand binding to demonstrate that subtype-specific differences originate at the level of allosteric coupling between ligand and transducer binding, and we use Systematic Protein Affinity Strength Modulation biosensors to show that Gq-specific residues in the 5 helix increase affinity for AngII-activated AT1R. We provide evidence that the 5 helix residue with the greatest effect on coupling makes interactions with AT1R intracellular loop 3 that were not resolved in a previously reported AT1R-Gq cryo-electron microscopy structure. These findings enhance our understanding of how AT1R differentially activates Gq and Gi and may ultimately guide pharmacological approaches to modulate certain G proteins downstream of AT1R and other GPCRs.

papers.title: A bacteriophage split DNA polymerase incorporates a sliding clamp-derived processivity subunit
papers.abstract: Viruses that infect bacteria, termed bacteriophages or phages, typically encode their own DNA replication machinery that rapidly generates many copies of the phage genomic DNA in an infected cell. Nucleus-forming phages of the chimallivirus family possess a distinctive repertoire of predicted DNA replication proteins, with two proteins annotated as DNA polymerases plus a DnaB-like replicative helicase, but lacking an identified primase or sliding clamp protein. Here, we demonstrate that in the Pseudomonas aeruginosa-infecting chimallivirus PhiKZ, the core DNA polymerase comprises a stable 1:1 complex of two DNA polymerase subunits, termed DNAPN and DNAPC. A 2.1 A resolution cryoelectron microscopy structure of this core complex reveals homology to other phage and bacterial B-family DNA polymerases. Next, we identify a direct but transient interaction between the core DNA polymerase complex and a third protein termed Rhc, which possesses an N-terminal RNase H domain and a C-terminal domain related to DNA sliding clamp proteins. Cryoelectron microscopy structures of a stabilized DNA polymerase-Rhc complex, and of this complex bound to a primer-template DNA, reveal a single Rhc subunit that cooperates with the DNA polymerase thumb domain to bind double-stranded DNA emerging from the DNA polymerase active site. While the Rhc RNase H domain is not resolved in our structures, this domain is situated such that it could degrade RNA associated with an incoming template DNA strand. In vitro primer-extension assays show that Rhc strongly boosts DNA polymerase activity, and that this boost relies on the Rhc-DNA polymerase interface we observe in our structures. Overall, our findings reveal a distinctive chimallivirus-specific DNA replication machine with an integrated DNA-binding subunit related to sliding clamp proteins, and a flexibly-linked RNase H domain.

papers.title: Global Regulatory Functions of the Human CCR4-NOT Complex in mRNA Deadenylation and Decay
papers.abstract: Shortening of the poly(A) tail initiates mRNA decay, and the human CCR4-NOT is the principal cytoplasmic deadenylase. Although its subunits have been defined, their functions have not been comprehensively evaluated in cells. We depleted each CCR4-NOT subunit and measured transcriptome-wide effects. CCR4-NOT regulated transcripts from thousands of genes, many of which associated with the complex in cells. Distinct groups of transcripts responded according to the modular organization of the complex, while subsets exhibited unique responses to specific subunits. Poly(A) tail analysis revealed that the CNOT7 and CNOT8 deadenylases are the predominant regulators of poly(A) tail length in these cells. CCR4-NOT targets were enriched in regulatory pathways including cell proliferation, apoptosis, stress responses, and cancer-related processes. Bioinformatic analysis identified sequence determinants and candidate recruitment factors associated with CCR4-NOT regulation. The results define the breadth and specificity of CCR4-NOT-mediated mRNA decay and provide a resource for dissecting regulatory mechanisms and biological roles.

papers.title: Taccalonolide AJ uncouples tubulin GTP hydrolysis from microtubule depolymerization
papers.abstract: Microtubules are dynamic polymers of tubulin subunits that are vital for a variety of eukaryotic cell functions, including intracellular trafficking and cell division. Microtubule-targeting drugs are among the oldest and most widely used chemotherapeutics. Despite their extensive use, the development and optimization of these drugs is hindered by our limited understanding of the molecular impacts on microtubules. Recent high-resolution structures have begun to explain how paclitaxel (Taxol) stabilizes microtubules: it reverses the hydrolysis-driven lateral strain at the microtubule seam and induces an expanded, GTP-like conformational state that promotes polymerization. In this work, we demonstrate that the microtubule-targeting natural product taccalonolide AJ (taccaAJ) stabilizes microtubules in a manner completely distinct from paclitaxel. Using cryo-EM, we show that taccaAJ stabilizes a compacted, post-GTP hydrolysis state, which is usually prone to depolymerization. In vitro assays show that taccaAJ-stabilized microtubules are more rigid than paclitaxel-stabilized microtubules, and reconstituted dynamics with taccaAJ exhibit increased rescue close to the plus-end. Finally, we use fluorescent biosensors for the compacted tubulin conformation to confirm that taccaAJ-stabilized microtubules in cells are compacted yet stable against depolymerization. We propose that taccaAJ preferentially binds a GDP lattice, promotes lateral interactions between protofilaments, and thus creates a rigid, stable microtubule in a compacted, post-GTP hydrolysis state.

papers.title: Proteomics of highly post-translationally modified proteins in kidney tubulointerstitium
papers.abstract: Kidney disease affects over 850 million people and leads to degradation of the kidney cortical compartments and kidney failure. Interstitial fibrosis and tubular atrophy (IFTA) is a universal feature of chronic kidney disease, yet the sequence of tubulointerstitial matrix protein (matrisome) changes that underlie the development and progression of IFTA are not fully understood. In particular, post-translational modifications which may stabilize key matrisome components and result in irreversible and functionally detrimental interstitial fibrosis or tubular basement membrane thickening, have yet to be characterized. Post-translational modifications (e.g., acetylation) have been shown to contribute to kidney diseases, yet they have not been investigated in chronic kidney disease progression. Herein, we established feasibility of matrisome protein quantification in the tubulointerstitium, with concurrent matrisome protein post-translational modification quantification, in archived diagnostic human kidney biopsies, using laser capture microdissection, liquid chromatography tandem mass spectrometry (LC-MS/MS), and bioinformatics analysis. In this pilot study, we focused on two conditions associated with IFTA progression: diabetic nephropathy and kidney transplantation. We examined both healthy and chronically damaged tubulointerstitium in two human kidney biopsies, one representing each condition. We identified signature protein markers of tubulointerstitium (e.g., UMOD, SLC12A1) in abundance, confirming sample composition, and observed uniformity in protein abundance across replicates from the same biopsies. We found increases in certain collagen isoforms (COL1A1, COL6A3) and other ancillary proteins in areas of IFTA. We also successfully quantified post-translational modifications, confirming that hydroxylproline was the most abundant modification in healthy tubulointerstitium from the kidney transplant biopsy, and that hydroxyllysine was also highly abundant and could be confidently quantitated on two collagen isoforms (COL1A1, COL4A2). Lastly, we performed power analysis to determine the required sample size to achieve significant power and false discovery rate. Several proteins exhibited large Hedge effect sizes in the tubulointerstitium (ANPEP, PRODH2), indicating their potential usefulness as fibrosis signatures. Our study is a first step toward comprehensive characterization of tubulointerstitial matrisome changes, including post-translational modifications seen with IFTA progression. Subsequent studies will potentially reveal new molecular markers of key early events in chronic kidney disease progression, and new therapeutic targets for mitigating this process. Data are available via ProteomeXchange identifier PXD079025.

papers.title: Synthetic inhibitors of pregnancy-associated plasma protein-A regulate IGF-1 signaling in vitro and in vivo
papers.abstract: Dysregulation of insulin-like growth factor (IGF) signaling contributes to diverse human diseases. Therapeutic strategies have largely targeted the IGF-1 receptor, but the complexity of the IGF system has limited their clinical efficacy. Pregnancy-associated plasma protein-A (PAPP-A) is a secreted metalloproteinase that regulates local IGF signaling through proteolytic cleavage of IGF-binding proteins (IGFBPs) and represents an attractive therapeutic target. Here, we report the first synthetic PAPP-A inhibitors designed to target the enzyme active site using an IGFBP-5-derived anchor sequence. Replacing the scissile bond with phosphinate or phosphonate moieties yielded potent and selective PAPP-A inhibitors. Cryo-electron microscopy revealed the molecular basis of inhibition and key active-site interactions. The compounds inhibited cleavage of IGFBP-4 and IGFBP-5, two physiological PAPP-A substrates. They suppressed IGF-1 signaling in A549 lung cancer cells, with efficacy comparable to the endogenous PAPP-A inhibitor stanniocalcin-1. They also inhibited Papp-aa-dependent IGF signaling and cell proliferation in wild-type and stc1a-/- mutant zebrafish in vivo in a dose-dependent manner. Together, these findings establish the first class of synthetic, selective PAPP-A inhibitors capable of modulating IGF signaling. They provide new chemical tools for studying and modulating pathological IGF signaling and offer new directions for developing PAPP-A-targeted therapeutic strategies.

papers.title: Mechanism of spike opening in a mammalian gammacoronavirus
papers.abstract: Coronavirus spike proteins mediate receptor binding and fusion and are key determinants of viral host range. To bind protein receptors, some CoV spikes undergo conformational changes termed opening, which expose the receptor-binding surface. Yet, the prerequisites and mechanism of spike opening remain poorly understood, especially outside of beta-CoVs, and many CoV spikes have been observed only in the closed conformation. The receptor specificities of gamma-CoVs, for which birds are natural hosts, await in-depth characterisation and their spikes have not been observed to open. Here, we report structures of the spike from an unusual mammalian gamma-CoV isolated from a beluga whale (BwCoV), in closed and open conformations, the latter with two S1B domains erect. BwCoV spike opening is associated with changes throughout S1 that resemble those observed in beta-CoV spikes and similarly propagate into destabilisation of the fusogenic S2 core. Furthermore, the BwCoV-S structure contains an additional density likely corresponding to a fatty acid, consistent with lipid binding stabilising the closed conformation through a pocket distinct from that identified for beta-CoVs. These structural insights reveal conserved principles regulating spike dynamics across coronavirus genera and support lipid binding as a potential modulatory mechanism of spike opening.

papers.title: Beyond RMSD: Deterministic Dlow Matching for Ultrafast and Physically Validated Transition-State Generation
papers.abstract: Transition state (TS) generation is typically evaluated by geometric similarity, yet low root-mean-square deviation (RMSD) does not establish first-order saddle-point character or reaction-path connectivity. Here we introduce Kairos-GFM, a deterministic equivariant flow-matching model that combines a two-dimensional reaction graph with the Kabsch-aligned mean of three-dimensional reactant and product geometries. Using 881 Transition1x reactions whose reference TSs passed strict saddle-point and bidirectional intrinsic reaction coordinate validation, Kairos-GFM generates one candidate in 0.0118 s with a median RMSD of 0.14 [A]. A hierarchical physical-validation framework--spanning reaction-center geometry, raw single-point energy, DFT saddle-point optimization, harmonic frequency analysis, and IRC endpoint matching reveals that low RMSD and saddle-point convergence do not guarantee the intended reaction channel. Kairos-GFM recovers the target channel in 75.94% of reactions, outperforming diffusion-based baselines but remaining below transport-based methods. These results position Kairos-GFM as a rapid initial-geometry generator for quantum-chemical refinement and provide a transferable validation standard that distinguishes geometric similarity from physical fidelity.

papers.title: The bacterial antiphage protein Tiamat is an ATPase and DNase whose homologs are found across the tree of life
papers.abstract: Bacteria and archaea encode hundreds of antiviral defense systems, some with homologs found in eukaryotic innate immunity. GHL ATPases like plant MORCs and prokaryotic Tiamat defend against viruses and phage, though their architecture and biochemical activities have remained unclear. Searching thousands of proteomes, we find Tiamat is rare in prokaryotes yet enriched across eukaryotes, including green plants, aquatic chordates, sponges, placozoans, and water molds. We resolve the central DUF3684 and flanking region into three predicted folds (TPR-like repeats, an uncharacterized conserved fold, and an inactive metalloprotease-like fold) that occupy the substrate-binding position of other GHL proteins. We show that purified Bacillus cereus Tiamat hydrolyzes ATP, inefficiently nicks duplex DNA, and cleaves single-stranded DNA site-specifically. We identify Tiamat-like proteins whose C-terminal nuclease is often swapped for helicases, peptidases, or other effectors. Additionally, we show Tiamat genes neighbor helicases, DNA methyltransferases, and nucleases, suggesting some Tiamats degrade foreign nucleic acid within a multi-component complex. Eukaryotic Tiamat homologs like the close Arabidopsis homolog NO VEIN and the distant human homolog SACSIN have acquired critical non-defense roles, leaving open whether these homologs remain antiviral or have been exapted.

papers.title: Sequence-specific and programmable catalytic degradation of extracellular microRNAs by membrane-anchored DNA nanomachines
papers.abstract: Extracellular microRNAs (miRNAs) contribute to metastasis through communication between tumour cells and their microenvironment, yet their sustained, sequence-selective depletion remains challenging. Here we report Programmable RNA-Intercepting Molecular Eraser (PRIME), a membrane-anchored DNA nanomachine that organizes miRNA recognition and catalytic degradation at the cell surface. A double-tetrahedral DNA scaffold positions a programmable recognition hairpin beside RNase H. Target binding generates an RNA/DNA hybrid for RNase H-mediated cleavage, and product release resets the hairpin for subsequent degradation cycles. Membrane-anchored PRIME depleted matched extracellular miRNAs by 70.6-89.4% across lung, breast and cervical cancer cell models. Multi-target PRIME (M-PRIME) inhibited migration by 71.3-96.0% in Transwell assays across these models. To evaluate its therapeutic potential, we established an orthotopic lung-tumour model and an early-intervention breast-cancer lung-colonization model in mice. Aptamer-directed M-PRIME combined with gemcitabine reduced pulmonary tumour burden by 74.5% in established lung tumours and 93.2% in the lung-colonization model. These effects were consistent with PRIME-mediated extracellular miRNA degradation, with circulating target miRNA levels reduced by 77.5-98.7% relative to gemcitabine alone. Together, these findings establish a programmable material strategy for sustained extracellular RNA depletion and support its potential to enhance chemotherapy in preclinical tumour models.

papers.title: Cryo-tides: synthetic peptides for cryo-EM grid preparation of multi-subunit protein complexes sensitive to the air-water interface
papers.abstract: Cryogenic electron microscopy (cryo-EM) has enabled rapid progress in structural biology throughout the last decade. However, cryo-EM sample preparation still represents a major bottleneck in high-resolution structure determination. Many proteins and macromolecular complexes interact with the air-water interface during sample preparation, which can cause protein denaturation, complex disassembly, and preferred particle orientation. Development of methods to alleviate these issues is an active field of investigation. However, a universally applicable solution to this problem has not been found so far. Here, we describe the simple and cost-effective usage of synthetic peptides with defined amino acid sequence to protect cryo-EM samples from complex disassembly and reduce preferred orientation. We show benefits during cryo-EM grid preparation of a large E3 ubiquitin ligase termed the anaphase-promoting complex (APC/C), and the small CDK11:cyclin L:SAP30BP complex.
